name: One Horse Open Slaw Burger - (Comes with slaw, no horse)

recipe.history:
Coleslaw traces its origins to the Netherlands, where a dish called "koolsla" — a compound of "kool" (cabbage) and "sla" (salad) — was recorded as far back as the late 18th century. Dutch settlers brought their culinary traditions to the American colonies, and this humble shredded cabbage salad quietly took root in the New World. In its earliest form, koolsla was dressed simply with butter, vinegar, and sometimes hot bacon fat, a far cry from the mayonnaise-laden versions we know today. Cabbage itself had long been prized across Europe and Asia for its durability, its ability to keep through harsh winters, and its versatility — fermented, braised, or raw — making coleslaw a natural expression of practical, peasant ingenuity elevated into something genuinely delicious.

Coleslaw found its way into American cuisine through both Dutch and German immigrant traditions, and by the 19th century it had become a staple of Southern cooking, picnic tables, and roadside diners from coast to coast. The introduction of commercially produced mayonnaise in the early 20th century transformed the dish — creamy slaw became the default, served alongside barbecue, fried chicken, and, inevitably, the hamburger. At drive-ins and burger stands throughout the mid-century, coleslaw was piled directly onto patties as a textural counterpoint: cool and crisp against hot, fatty beef. The combination made intuitive sense — the acidity of the slaw cut through richness, the crunch contrasted with a yielding bun, and the creaminess tied every element together. It became a regional signature across the American South and Midwest, a tradition as honest and unpretentious as the hamburger itself.

I remember the first time I encountered a slaw burger as something more than a curiosity. It was at a county fair somewhere in the Carolina foothills, late August, the air thick and sugary with funnel cake smoke. A hand-painted sign read simply "Slaw Burger — $3" and I ordered one without thinking, more out of hunger than conviction. The woman behind the counter built it without ceremony: a smashed patty, a hill of creamy slaw, a soft bun pressed flat in her palm. I ate it standing at a folding table while a bluegrass band tuned up nearby. Something about that combination — the cold crunch of cabbage, the warm give of the beef, the sweetness of the dressing against the salt — felt like a revelation that had been hiding in plain sight my entire life. That burger has lived in the back of my mind ever since, a quiet benchmark against which I measure every slaw burger that follows.

A burger cooked to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit at the center — is not a preference; it is the correct answer to the question of how a burger should be cooked. At that temperature, the muscle fibers have relaxed just enough to release their juices without surrendering them entirely. The fat has begun to render, basting the interior of the patty from within. The crust can be deep and crackling on the outside while the center remains pink, yielding, and trembling with moisture. To cook a burger beyond this point is to trade flavor for the illusion of safety — an illusion, because properly sourced, freshly ground beef presents negligible risk and maximum reward when treated with respect. Well-done beef is dry beef; it is a different food entirely, one that requires sauces and condiments to compensate for what the heat has taken away. Medium rare requires nothing to apologize for. It is complete on its own terms, and every topping you add — including a generous heap of cold, creamy coleslaw — is there to celebrate it, not rescue it.
ingredients: 3 1/2 cups (440g) bread flour, plus more for dusting
1 egg yolk + 1 tablespoon milk, for egg wash
1 1/2 lbs (680g) freshly ground beef, 80/20 chuck blend
1 tablespoon neutral oil (such as canola or vegetable)
3 cups (about 1/2 small head) green cabbage, finely shredded
1 cup (about 1/4 head) red cabbage, finely shredded
4 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened (for toasting buns)
4 slices American or mild cheddar cheese (optional)
instructions: 1. Make the bun dough: In a large bowl or the bowl of a stand mixer, combine the warmed milk, yeast, and sugar. Let sit for 5 minutes until foamy. Add the egg, softened butter, and salt. Add the bread flour in two additions and mix on medium speed with a dough hook (or knead by hand) for 8–10 minutes, until the dough is smooth, soft, and slightly tacky but not sticky.
2. First rise: Shape the dough into a ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap or a damp towel, and let rise in a warm spot for 1 to 1.5 hours, until doubled in size.

3. Shape the buns: Punch down the dough and divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 150g each). Shape each into a tight, smooth ball by tucking the edges underneath and rolling on a clean surface. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing them at least 3 inches apart. Gently flatten each ball to about 3/4-inch thickness.
4. Second rise: Cover the shaped buns loosely with plastic wrap and let proof for 45–60 minutes at room temperature, until noticeably puffed and pillowy.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Whisk together the egg yolk and 1 tablespoon milk. Brush the tops of the buns gently with the egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds if using.
6. Bake the buns for 16–20 minutes, until deep golden brown on top. Transfer to a wire rack and let cool completely before slicing.

7. Make the coleslaw: In a large bowl, combine the shredded green cabbage, red cabbage, grated carrot, and green onions. In a separate small bowl, whisk together the mayonnaise, apple cider vinegar, sugar, Dijon mustard, celery seed, salt, and pepper until smooth.

8. Pour the dressing over the cabbage mixture and toss thoroughly to coat every strand. Taste and adjust seasoning — add more vinegar for tang, sugar for sweetness, or salt as needed. Cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes (and up to 4 hours) to allow the flavors to meld and the cabbage to soften slightly while retaining its crunch.

9. Form the patties: Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (approximately 170g each). Handle the meat as little as possible — gently shape each portion into a patty about 3/4 inch thick and slightly wider than your buns (they will shrink during cooking). Use your thumb to press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty to prevent doming. Season generously on both sides with salt, black pepper, and garlic powder immediately before cooking.

10. Cook the patties to medium rare: Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until smoking. Add the oil and butter. Place the patties in the pan and do not press them down. Cook undisturbed for 3 minutes to develop a deep, dark crust. Flip once and cook for an additional 2–2.5 minutes. Check the internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer — you are looking for 130–135°F (54–57°C) at the center. This is medium rare and the only correct endpoint. If adding cheese, lay a slice on each patty in the last 30 seconds and tent the pan loosely with foil to melt.

11. Rest the patties: Transfer the cooked patties to a wire rack or plate and let them rest uncovered for 3–4 minutes. The residual heat will carry the internal temperature up slightly while the juices redistribute throughout the meat. Do not skip this step.

12. Toast the buns: While the patties rest, split the buns and spread the cut sides with softened butter. Toast cut-side down in the same skillet over medium heat for 1–2 minutes until golden and lightly crisped.

13. Assemble the burgers: On the bottom bun, spread a thin line of yellow mustard if desired and layer a few dill pickle slices. Place the cooked patty (with melted cheese if using) on top. Pile a generous, unapologetic mound of cold coleslaw directly onto the patty — do not be shy here, the cold-against-hot contrast is the entire point of this burger. Cap with the top bun, press down gently, and serve immediately.
